questions.explanation: A sloping expiratory CO₂ upstroke suggests obstructed gas emptying, and a cleft in the plateau can reflect spontaneous respiratory effort. Gradually rising end-tidal CO₂ is less specific and requires assessment of ventilation, perfusion, metabolism, and equipment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3e, Ch. 10, Capnography (chapter-associated; exact question-specific printed page and full answer set not verified)

questions.stem: Which conditions can reduce pulmonary blood flow, increase alveolar dead space, and lower end-tidal CO₂? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Pulmonary embolism, hypovolemia, and cardiac tamponade can each reduce perfusion of ventilated alveoli, increasing alveolar dead space and lowering end-tidal CO₂. End-tidal values must still be interpreted with ventilation and other clinical findings.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 10, printed p. 248 (complete revised question and answer set independently verified)

questions.stem: Which hemoglobin species are included in the denominator of fractional saturation but not functional saturation? Select 2.
questions.explanation: Functional saturation divides oxyhemoglobin by oxyhemoglobin plus reduced hemoglobin. Fractional saturation adds carboxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin to the denominator, so those two species distinguish the calculations.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 11, printed p. 253 (complete revised question and answer set independently verified)

questions.stem: Which factors can interfere with conventional pulse oximeter accuracy or signal acquisition? Select 3.
options: Supine position on a normal limb
questions.explanation: Intravenous dyes alter optical absorbance, while hypothermia and poor perfusion can diminish the pulsatile signal needed for a reading. Fetal hemoglobin generally has little effect on conventional two-wavelength pulse oximetry.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 11, printed pp. 258–260 (complete revised question and answer set independently verified)

questions.stem: A volume-time curve doesn't return to baseline. Which causes fit? Select 2.
questions.explanation: An expiratory volume-time curve that fails to return to baseline may reflect trapped gas from incomplete exhalation or a loss of measured expiratory volume through a leak. Interpret it with flow, pressure, and circuit checks.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3e, Ch. 8, Respiratory Gas Monitoring (chapter-associated; exact question-specific printed page and full answer set not verified)

questions.stem: Which clinical uses of capnography are supported by the textbook? Select 2.
options: Keeping ventilation stable during transport with raised ICP
questions.explanation: End-tidal CO₂ trends help assess pulmonary blood flow and compression effectiveness during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Capnography also helps identify dangerous ventilation changes during transport, especially when intracranial pressure makes stable CO₂ control important.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 10, printed pp. 247–248 (complete revised question and answer set independently verified)

questions.stem: Which promote turbulent flow? Select 3.
questions.explanation: High gas velocity, narrowing from secretions, and abrupt bends promote disturbed or turbulent flow. These effects raise resistance and can increase the pressure needed for ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3e, Ch. 8, Respiratory Gas Monitoring (chapter-associated; exact question-specific printed page and full answer set not verified)

questions.stem: On this analyzer response graph, which numbered interval is the transit (delay) time?
questions.explanation: Interval 1 spans the delay between the step change at point 3 and the first analyzer response. That is the transit or sampling delay; the image confirms the labeled interval.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3e, Ch. 8, Respiratory Gas Monitoring (chapter-associated; exact question-specific printed page and full answer set not verified)

questions.stem: Which numbered interval on this graph depends mainly on the analyzer's own speed of reaction?
questions.explanation: Interval 2 shows how quickly the analyzer signal rises after the sample reaches the sensor. This is the analyzer rise time, confirmed by the labeled response graph.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3e, Ch. 8, Respiratory Gas Monitoring (chapter-associated; exact question-specific printed page and full answer set not verified)

questions.stem: A longer sampling line is installed. Which numbered part of this graph lengthens?
questions.explanation: A longer sampling line increases the time for gas to reach a remote analyzer, represented by interval 1. It does not primarily alter the sensor's intrinsic rise time.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3e, Ch. 8, Respiratory Gas Monitoring (chapter-associated; exact question-specific printed page and full answer set not verified)

questions.stem: A sidestream analyzer has a transit delay of 2.5 seconds and a rise time of 0.4 seconds. What is its total response time?
questions.explanation: Total response time combines sampling-line transit delay and analyzer rise time. Adding 2.5 and 0.4 seconds gives 2.9 seconds.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 10, printed p. 245 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: A sidestream analyzer has a total response time of 3.2 seconds and a rise time of 0.5 seconds. What is its transit delay?
questions.explanation: Transit delay is the total response time minus analyzer rise time. Subtracting 0.5 from 3.2 seconds gives 2.7 seconds.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 10, printed p. 245 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: In panel A, the numbered device is which type of analyzer?
questions.explanation: Panel A places the sensor directly in the airway gas stream at component 1, making it a mainstream analyzer. The supplied diagram shows no remote sample transport line for this sensor.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3e, Ch. 8, Respiratory Gas Monitoring (chapter-associated; exact question-specific printed page and full answer set not verified)

questions.stem: In panel B, what is numbered component 3 most likely?
options: An in-line mainstream sensor at the airway
A water trap leading to the analyzer
questions.explanation: In panel B, the airway sample travels through tubing to a remote analyzer. Component 3 is the downstream sampling/water-trap assembly, as indicated by the supplied diagram.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3e, Ch. 8, Respiratory Gas Monitoring (chapter-associated; exact question-specific printed page and full answer set not verified)

questions.stem: Compared with panel A, panel B will show which characteristic?
options: Larger added dead space at the airway
A longer delay before changes appear
More interference from blood at the sensor
questions.explanation: Panel B uses sidestream sampling, so the sampled gas must travel to a remote analyzer before measurement. Its transport delay is generally greater than panel A's mainstream sensor.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3e, Ch. 8, Respiratory Gas Monitoring (chapter-associated; exact question-specific printed page and full answer set not verified)

questions.stem: Thick secretions coat the airway adapter. Which panel's readings are most directly affected?
questions.explanation: Panel A has an optical sensor in the airway adapter. Secretions or condensation on that sensor can interfere directly with its light-based measurement.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3e, Ch. 8, Respiratory Gas Monitoring (chapter-associated; exact question-specific printed page and full answer set not verified)

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes mainstream capnography from sidestream sampling?
options: It always requires a water trap
It has a longer sampling delay than sidestream systems
It aspirates respiratory gas through sample tubing
It measures carbon dioxide directly at the airway without aspirating gas
questions.explanation: A mainstream capnograph measures carbon dioxide in gas passing through an airway adapter without removing a gas sample. Sidestream systems aspirate gas through sampling tubing and introduce transport delay; disposable adapters are available but are not a defining feature of mainstream measurement.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 240–241

questions.stem: Why can sidestream capnography underestimate end-tidal CO₂ at very high respiratory rates?
options: Short breaths outpace the analyzer’s response
The water trap fills faster at high rates
Fresh gas floods the sampling line
questions.explanation: Rapid breaths may not remain at the sampling site long enough for the sidestream analyzer to respond fully. Sampling delay and analyzer rise time can therefore distort or underestimate the measured end-tidal CO₂.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 10, printed p. 245 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: At sea level, an inspired mixture with 1% sevoflurane exerts about what partial pressure of sevo?
questions.explanation: Partial pressure equals fractional concentration multiplied by total gas pressure. For 1% sevoflurane at 760 mmHg, 0.01 × 760 = 7.6 mmHg.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 199

questions.stem: At an altitude where barometric pressure is 630 mmHg, 21% O2 exerts about what partial pressure (dry gas)?
questions.explanation: In a dry mixture, oxygen partial pressure is its fraction multiplied by barometric pressure. At 630 mmHg, 0.21 × 630 = 132.3 mmHg, approximately 132 mmHg.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 199

questions.stem: For which type of gas mixture is Dalton's law of partial pressures directly applicable?
questions.explanation: Dalton's law states that the total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of its component gases. The keyed nonreacting-gas mixture fits this additive model; chemically reacting substances can change the mixture's composition.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed p. 199 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: In a mixture of O2, N2O, and sevo at 760 mmHg, O2 exerts 250 mmHg and N2O 494 mmHg. What does sevo exert?
questions.explanation: The individual partial pressures must sum to the total pressure. With only the three stated gases present, sevoflurane contributes 760 − 250 − 494 = 16 mmHg.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 199

questions.stem: Which analysis method separates gas molecules into ions by mass?
questions.explanation: Mass spectrometry ionizes the sample and separates the resulting charged particles by mass-to-charge ratio. Their relative abundance identifies and quantifies components of the gas mixture.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 200

questions.stem: Infrared analyzers report which quantity?
questions.explanation: Infrared absorption depends on the number of absorbing gas molecules in the measurement chamber and therefore measures partial pressure. A monitor may convert that measurement to a displayed volume percentage.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed pp. 199–200

questions.stem: Which method relies on light scattered with a change in energy by gas molecules?
questions.explanation: Raman scattering produces scattered light at wavelengths different from the incident light. These shifts are characteristic of particular gases and allow their identification and measurement.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 204

questions.stem: Which factor can make capnometer readings inaccurate?
questions.explanation: Water vapor and condensation can affect CO₂ measurement. Water handling and heated or coated optical windows help limit errors, while dry-versus-saturated reporting conditions also affect the value.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed pp. 204–205

questions.stem: A colorimetric detector shows yellow on expiration and purple on inspiration for six breaths. What does this confirm?
options: Correct depth of the tube above the carina
questions.explanation: A repeated yellow-to-purple change indicates exhaled CO₂ followed by inspired gas with little CO₂, supporting tracheal placement. Observation over several breaths reduces the risk of mistaking transient gastric CO₂ for sustained ventilation; it does not establish tube depth or oxygenation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 205; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 316

questions.stem: When waveform capnography is unavailable, what can a qualitative colorimetric CO₂ detector provide?
options: It measures the exact end-tidal CO₂ value
It replaces waveform capnography for continuous ventilation monitoring
It confirms tube placement with certainty in every low-flow state
It provides a qualitative indication of exhaled CO₂
questions.explanation: A qualitative colorimetric detector changes color in response to exhaled CO₂ and can help assess airway placement when a capnograph fails. It does not provide an exact end-tidal value or replace continuous waveform monitoring, and low-perfusion states may limit interpretation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 8, printed pp 205, 215 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: A galvanic O2 cell gradually reads lower over months despite correct FiO2. Why?
options: Nitrogen poisons the cell over time
The lead anode is consumed over time
questions.explanation: A galvanic oxygen cell consumes its anode during the electrochemical reaction. Its output and calibration can therefore change as the cell ages, so a gradually low reading may reflect a depleted cell rather than a true fall in FiO₂.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed pp. 207, 209

questions.stem: Where is a galvanic cell's membrane exposed?
options: To the gas in the circuit
questions.explanation: The cell’s oxygen-permeable membrane is exposed to gas in the breathing circuit. Oxygen diffuses through it into the electrolyte, generating a signal related to oxygen partial pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 207

questions.stem: Which property makes O2 detectable by a paramagnetic analyzer?
questions.explanation: Oxygen has two unpaired electrons, making it attracted to a magnetic field. Paramagnetic analyzers use this property to distinguish oxygen from most other respiratory gases.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 207

questions.stem: Capnography confirms CO2 after intubation, but SpO2 drifts down and left chest rise is absent. What is the best next step?
options: Accept placement because CO2 is present
Increase FiO2 and continue the case
Pull back slightly and listen bilaterally
Replace the CO2 detector and recheck
questions.explanation: Exhaled CO₂ confirms ventilation but does not exclude endobronchial intubation. Loss of left-sided chest movement after intubation warrants reassessment of tube depth and bilateral ventilation; withdrawal may correct an excessively deep tube.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 232; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 250

questions.stem: The oxygram mirrors the capnogram. During exhalation, what does the oxygram show?
questions.explanation: During oxygen uptake, expired gas contains less oxygen than inspired gas. The oxygram therefore falls during expiration as the capnogram rises with exhaled CO₂.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed pp. 208–209

questions.stem: Rising end-tidal N2 during a sitting craniotomy most suggests what?
questions.explanation: Air entering the venous circulation introduces nitrogen that can subsequently appear in exhaled gas. A rising end-tidal nitrogen concentration in this setting therefore raises concern for venous air embolism, although leaks and sampling problems also require consideration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 213

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, which end-tidal measure shows denitrogenation?
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation replaces nitrogen in the lungs with oxygen. Falling end-tidal nitrogen therefore indicates progressive denitrogenation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 213

questions.stem: Where nitrogen monitoring isn't available, which measures are used instead?
questions.explanation: End-tidal oxygen helps assess preoxygenation, while changes in end-tidal CO₂ can help detect reduced pulmonary perfusion associated with air embolism. These measurements address different purposes and do not directly measure nitrogen.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 213

questions.stem: A patient receives 0.6 MAC sevo with 0.5 MAC N2O. What is the total MAC?
questions.explanation: MAC fractions of nitrous oxide and potent inhaled agents are additive in this calculation. Thus 0.6 MAC sevoflurane plus 0.5 MAC nitrous oxide equals 1.1 MAC.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 213

questions.stem: At emergence, which step lowers circuit agent concentration fastest?
questions.explanation: Turning the vaporizer off stops adding fresh anesthetic vapor. High fresh-gas flow then replaces circuit gas more rapidly and reduces rebreathing, lowering circuit agent concentration faster than low flow.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 270

questions.stem: Tidal volume falls and airway pressure falls together. Which cause fits best?
questions.explanation: A leak or disconnection can prevent the circuit from building pressure and reduce the volume returned from the patient. Simultaneous falls in pressure and tidal volume therefore fit a circuit-integrity problem.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Airway pressure rises while delivered volume is unchanged in volume control. Which problem fits?
options: A kink or other added resistance
A leak around the ETT cuff
questions.explanation: In volume control, the ventilator may maintain volume by generating greater pressure against increased resistance. A kink or obstruction in the gas pathway therefore fits increased airway pressure with unchanged delivered volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: When evaluating ventilation, why think about dead space with tidal volume?
options: Dead space adds to alveolar ventilation
Part of each breath isn’t exchanged
questions.explanation: Dead-space ventilation is the portion of each tidal breath that does not participate in gas exchange. Tidal volume must therefore be considered together with dead space when estimating effective alveolar ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 245

questions.stem: Which panel shows laminar flow?
questions.explanation: Panel A shows smooth, parallel gas movement consistent with laminar flow. Panel B shows irregular paths that represent turbulent flow.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed pp. 224–225

questions.stem: A secretion partially blocks an ETT. Flow changes from panel A toward which pattern?
questions.explanation: Secretions narrow and disrupt the flow pathway, promoting turbulent flow. In the supplied schematic, this shifts the pattern toward panel B rather than the smooth parallel paths in panel A.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed pp. 224–225

questions.stem: Which change would push flow from panel B back toward panel A?
options: Switching to a denser gas mix
Lower flow through a wider, straighter path
Adding a sharp bend to the tubing
Higher flow through the same narrowed path
questions.explanation: Lower flow through a wider, straighter pathway reduces conditions that promote turbulence. This favors the smoother pattern depicted in panel A.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed pp. 224–225; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 266

questions.stem: Gas flow monitoring is based on smoothness and which other principles?
options: Conservation of charge and momentum only
questions.explanation: Flow analysis uses continuity and conservation of mass: gas entering a defined pathway must be accounted for as gas leaving or accumulating within it. These principles connect measured velocity, cross-sectional area, and volume flow.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 224

questions.stem: Which gas property helps determine the transition from laminar to turbulent flow?
questions.explanation: Viscosity influences the transition between laminar and turbulent flow together with gas density, velocity, and pathway geometry. It is therefore one of the relevant gas properties in the critical-velocity relationship.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed pp. 224–225

questions.stem: Flowmeters are used to measure what in anesthesia?
options: Gas supply flows and circuit tidal ventilation
Arterial blood gas values during surgery
questions.explanation: Flowmeters are used both to meter gases supplied to an anesthesia system and to measure changing respiratory flows in the breathing circuit. Integrating respiratory flow over time provides tidal volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 225

questions.stem: A cracked O2 rotameter tube leaks gas. What happens to delivered O2?
options: Less O2 is delivered than indicated
More O2 is delivered than indicated
questions.explanation: A cracked oxygen flowmeter can allow oxygen to escape and produce a hypoxic mixture. The amount delivered relative to the indicated value depends on the leak location and configuration, so the precise display-versus-delivery claim remains conditional.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 225

questions.stem: A pneumotachometer determines flow from:
options: Pressure drop across a known resistance
Height of a float in a tube
Infrared absorption by the flowing gas
questions.explanation: A pneumotachometer measures the pressure difference across a known resistance to infer flow. Its calibration depends on the characteristics of the resistance element and gas.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 226

questions.stem: Spirometry helps distinguish which etiologies?
questions.explanation: Spirometry measures ventilatory function and can help identify a respiratory contribution to symptoms such as dyspnea. The source identifies distinguishing respiratory from cardiac etiologies as an application, rather than a standalone definitive diagnosis.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 230

questions.stem: FEV1/FVC is reduced. Which disease pattern does this suggest?
questions.explanation: A reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio suggests airflow obstruction because the first-second expired volume falls disproportionately. Restrictive disease can reduce vital capacity while preserving the ratio.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 637

questions.stem: On a volume-time curve, exhalation appears as what?
questions.explanation: A conventional ventilator volume-time display rises as inspired volume enters the lungs. During exhalation the volume falls toward baseline, producing a downslope.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 230

questions.stem: A volume-time curve returns below baseline every breath. What is the most likely equipment explanation?
questions.explanation: A volume-time curve extending below baseline can reflect inaccurate flow-transducer calibration. Active exhalation can also produce this appearance, so calibration is the best equipment explanation among these choices rather than the only possible cause.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: A volume-time curve fails to return to baseline. Which two causes fit?
questions.explanation: Failure of the expiratory volume-time curve to reach baseline can indicate incomplete emptying or an expiratory limb leak. Correlating volume with expiratory flow and the circuit check helps distinguish these causes.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: A patient with severe COPD develops panel B. Which change helps most?
questions.explanation: Panel B shows expiratory volume remaining above baseline, consistent with incomplete emptying in this COPD scenario. Lengthening expiration gives obstructed lungs more time to empty and can reduce dynamic hyperinflation; a leak remains another possible cause of this curve.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644

questions.stem: In panel C, which ventilator change best addresses the problem?
questions.explanation: In the third tracing, expiration appears interrupted before flow smoothly reaches zero, suggesting incomplete emptying. More expiratory time can help, but the supplied image lacks panel letters and axis labels, so the reference to panel C needs clarification.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Which pressure-volume loop shows spontaneous breathing?
questions.explanation: Loop C includes a negative-pressure inspiratory portion, the characteristic pattern of spontaneous breathing in the conventional display. Positive-pressure ventilation generally produces loops on the positive-pressure side.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: Which loop shows PEEP?
questions.explanation: Loop D is displaced to a positive end-expiratory pressure rather than beginning at zero. This rightward baseline shift represents PEEP on the conventional pressure-volume axes.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: Compared with loop A, loop B indicates what change?
questions.explanation: Loop B has a lower volume change for a given pressure change than loop A. Its flatter slope therefore indicates decreased compliance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 232

questions.stem: After intubation, the loop shifts from A to B. Which equipment-related cause should you check first?
questions.explanation: Endobronchial intubation can reduce the ventilated lung volume and shift the pressure-volume loop toward lower volume at higher pressure. After intubation, this pattern warrants checking tube depth and bilateral ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 232

questions.stem: What determines the normal shape of a pressure-volume loop?
questions.explanation: Pressure-volume loop shape depends on how the breath is delivered, including ventilation mode and flow pattern. Normal interpretation therefore begins with the mode and settings rather than assuming one universal loop.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 231

questions.stem: A slower sampling system mainly distorts which numbered segment of this capnogram?
questions.explanation: Segment 2 is the expiratory upstroke as CO₂-rich gas reaches the sensor. Slow sampling or analyzer response can make this rise less steep and distort that segment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242

questions.stem: In the supplied capnogram, which numbered segment represents the initial exhalation of carbon dioxide–free gas from the anatomic and apparatus dead space?
questions.explanation: Phase I of the capnogram is the flat initial expiratory baseline, when carbon dioxide–free gas from the apparatus and anatomic dead space passes the sensor. The supplied figure labels this segment 1; segment 2 is the rising phase II upstroke as alveolar gas appears.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242

questions.stem: Which capnography panel most suggests esophageal intubation?
questions.explanation: Panel A shows CO₂ declining over successive breaths until little remains. This can occur when an esophageal tube initially detects trapped gastric CO₂ that is then washed out, unlike sustained alveolar CO₂.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 241–242

questions.stem: Which panel shows a progressively rising baseline?
questions.explanation: Panel D shows the inspiratory baseline rising on successive breaths. This indicates increasing inspired CO₂ and raises concern for rebreathing, which requires assessment of the circuit and valves.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242

questions.stem: Panel C appears during a hip arthroplasty after cementing, with falling BP. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: An embolic reduction in pulmonary blood flow increases alveolar dead space and can lower end-tidal CO₂ despite continued ventilation. The timing after cementing and falling blood pressure make embolism a leading concern, although the tracing alone is not diagnostic.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 244, 249

questions.stem: Panel B occurs with airway pressure also dropping to zero. FIRST action?
questions.explanation: Panel B shows abrupt loss of exhaled CO₂, and a simultaneous fall in airway pressure supports disconnection or a major leak. Immediately assess ventilation and check the airway and circuit connections.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 241; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Panel B occurs, but airway pressures and tidal volumes are unchanged. What should be considered?
options: A circuit disconnection at the Y-piece
Arrest or loss of pulmonary blood flow
questions.explanation: If exhaled CO₂ disappears while delivered volume and airway pressure are maintained, severely reduced pulmonary blood flow must be considered. Cardiac arrest can produce this pattern, so assess circulation promptly while also checking the airway and sampling system.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 241, 248–249

questions.stem: Which panel requires checking the absorbent and unidirectional valves?
questions.explanation: Panel D shows progressively increasing inspired CO₂, indicating rebreathing. Check the CO₂ absorbent and unidirectional valves because either can allow exhaled CO₂ to return to the patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242

questions.stem: A patient with panel A gets albuterol and improves. How should the waveform change?
questions.explanation: Panel A has a slanted expiratory upstroke consistent with airflow obstruction. As bronchospasm improves, expiration becomes less obstructed and the tracing should become more square, with a steeper upstroke and flatter plateau.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242

questions.stem: Why is capnography useful in neurosurgical cases?
questions.explanation: Changes in arterial CO₂ alter cerebral blood flow: hypercarbia increases it, while hypocarbia decreases it. Capnography helps follow ventilation trends but does not directly measure intracranial pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 247

questions.stem: EtCO2 rises from 35 to 55 mmHg over 15 minutes with unchanged ventilation, HR rising, and temp climbing. What should you suspect?
options: A circuit leak diluting the sample
questions.explanation: Increasing CO₂ despite unchanged ventilation can reflect increased metabolic CO₂ production. Rising heart rate and temperature strengthen concern for a hypermetabolic process, including malignant hyperthermia in the appropriate setting; the pattern alone is not diagnostic.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Ventilation that doesn't participate in gas exchange is called:
questions.explanation: Dead-space ventilation is the portion of each breath that does not participate in gas exchange. It is therefore also called wasted ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 245

questions.stem: Which equation describes physiologic dead space components?
options: Minute ventilation − alveolar ventilation per breath only
Airway dead space + alveolar dead space
questions.explanation: Physiologic dead space is the sum of airway dead space and alveolar dead space. The former is conducting-airway volume, while the latter represents ventilated alveoli that do not effectively exchange gas.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 245

questions.stem: Massive hemorrhage lowers EtCO2 before BP falls much. Why?
options: Blood loss increases the body’s CO2 production
Lower lung perfusion raises alveolar dead space
Hemorrhage raises PaCO2 but not EtCO2
questions.explanation: Blood loss can reduce pulmonary perfusion, leaving more alveolar ventilation unmatched to blood flow. This increased dead-space fraction can lower end-tidal CO₂ even when ventilation is unchanged.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 248–249

questions.stem: Which condition can reduce pulmonary perfusion, increase alveolar dead space, and lower end-tidal CO₂?
questions.explanation: Hypovolemia can reduce pulmonary blood flow, creating ventilated but underperfused alveoli and lowering end-tidal CO₂. Increased CO₂ production or rebreathing from exhausted absorbent does not explain this perfusion-related fall.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 10, printed pp. 248–249 (complete revised question and answer set independently verified)

questions.stem: During CPR, why is PETCO2 low?
questions.explanation: Chest compressions generally produce less pulmonary blood flow than normal cardiac contraction. Less CO₂ reaches ventilated alveoli, so end-tidal CO₂ is often low during CPR.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248

questions.stem: PETCO2 during CPR rises abruptly from 12 to 38 mmHg. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: Return of spontaneous circulation increases pulmonary blood flow and CO₂ delivery to the lungs. A sudden sustained rise in end-tidal CO₂ during CPR therefore suggests restored circulation and should prompt clinical assessment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248

questions.stem: In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), how can capnography contribute to assessment during positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) titration?
options: To help find the best PEEP
questions.explanation: CO₂ monitoring can help assess how PEEP changes dead space and V/Q matching in ARDS. It is an adjunct to PEEP titration and does not independently diagnose ARDS or replace oxygenation and hemodynamic assessment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248

questions.stem: During weaning from mechanical ventilation, which measurement can complement capnography when arterial CO₂ needs confirmation?
questions.explanation: End-tidal and arterial CO₂ can diverge substantially during critical illness and ventilator weaning. Periodic arterial blood gases remain useful when the gradient is unknown or changing, particularly when precise PaCO₂ is needed.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248

questions.stem: During deep sedation without an airway, EtCO2 waveform flattens while chest movement continues. What is the most likely problem?
questions.explanation: Chest movement can continue despite little effective airflow when the airway is obstructed. A flat sampled CO₂ waveform therefore requires immediate assessment of airway patency and ventilation, while checking the sampling interface as well.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 249

questions.stem: During procedural sedation, which bedside assessment remains essential alongside capnography?
questions.explanation: Capnography complements direct observation and examination of the patient. Inspection, palpation, and auscultation remain essential because a monitor or sampling system can fail.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 249

questions.stem: A patient has 10% COHb, 87% O2Hb, 3% RHb. What is the fractional O2Hb?
questions.explanation: Fractional saturation includes all hemoglobin species in the denominator. With 87% O₂Hb, 3% reduced Hb, and 10% COHb, fractional O₂Hb is 87%.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: Using the same values (10% COHb, 87% O2Hb, 3% RHb), what is the functional saturation?
questions.explanation: Functional saturation includes only oxyhemoglobin and reduced hemoglobin in the denominator. Here 87/(87 + 3) × 100 = 96.7%, approximately 97%, despite the presence of COHb.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: Hb 15 g/dL, SaO2 98%, PaO2 95 mmHg. Approximate CaO2?
questions.explanation: Assuming no important dyshemoglobins, CaO₂ ≈ 1.34 × 15 × 0.98 + 0.003 × 95 = 19.98 mL O₂/dL. Almost all of this approximately 20 mL/dL is hemoglobin-bound oxygen.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: Assuming other variables are unchanged and hemoglobin remains fully saturated, which change produces the greatest increase in arterial oxygen content (CaO₂)?
options: Raising FiO2 from 0.4 to 0.5 with SaO2 at 100%
questions.explanation: The arterial oxygen-content equation is CaO₂ = 1.34 × Hb × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂. Increasing hemoglobin from 8 to 12 g/dL adds approximately 5.36 mL O₂/dL at full saturation, far exceeding the dissolved-oxygen gain from the listed PaO₂ changes.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 11, printed p. 253 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Doubling PaO2 from 100 to 200 mmHg at SaO2 100% raises CaO2 by about how much?
questions.explanation: With hemoglobin already fully saturated and otherwise unchanged, the added oxygen is dissolved in plasma. The increase is 0.003 × (200 − 100) = 0.3 mL O₂/dL.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: In the CaO2 equation, 1.34 represents what?
options: mL O2 per gram of saturated Hb
questions.explanation: The coefficient 1.34 represents the approximate milliliters of oxygen carried per gram of fully saturated hemoglobin. Multiplying it by Hb concentration and fractional saturation gives the hemoglobin-bound oxygen content.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: In this pulse oximetry schematic, which numbered element represents path length?
questions.explanation: Element 3 marks the distance light travels through the absorbing material. This is the optical path length in the Beer–Lambert relationship.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 255–256

questions.stem: Which numbered element contains the absorbing substance whose concentration is measured?
questions.explanation: Element 2 is the absorbing medium through which the light passes. Its absorbing substances and their concentrations influence how much light reaches the detector.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 255–256

questions.stem: Swelling of the finger increases numbered element 3. Per Beer-Lambert, absorbance:
questions.explanation: For unchanged concentration and absorption coefficient, increasing optical path length increases absorbance and reduces transmitted light. This simplified relationship does not by itself predict the displayed SpO₂, which also depends on pulsatile signals and wavelength ratios.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 255–256

questions.stem: In A = εcl, what is "ε"?
questions.explanation: ε is the absorption or extinction coefficient of the substance at the selected wavelength. It describes how strongly the substance absorbs light for a given concentration and path length.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 256

questions.stem: After methylene blue injection, SpO2 drops briefly to 85% with a normal ABG. Why?
options: The dye absorbs light: falsely low SpO2
Probe placed on a cold finger
questions.explanation: Methylene blue absorbs light used by conventional pulse oximeters and can cause a transient falsely low SpO₂. The reading should be interpreted with the clinical picture and appropriate blood-gas or CO-oximetry information.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 258

questions.stem: A cold, vasoconstricted patient has an erratic SpO2 signal. Which listed factors explain it?
questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction reduces pulsatile blood flow at the probe, weakening the arterial optical signal. A cold, poorly perfused finger can therefore produce an erratic or unreliable SpO₂ reading.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 259–260

questions.stem: What can be concluded about the direction of pulse-oximeter bias in patients with sickle cell disease from the conflicting evidence?
questions.explanation: The text describes conflicting findings about pulse-oximeter accuracy in sickle cell disease, partly because reference methods and dissociation curves differ. It therefore does not support an always-high or always-low error direction.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 258

questions.stem: Why does ECG synchronization help pulse oximetry?
options: It times sampling to arterial pulses
questions.explanation: ECG synchronization uses heart-rate timing to help distinguish pulse-related signals from motion artifact. The text describes it as a historical strategy that was not particularly successful and was abandoned in later models, rather than a universal feature.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 260

questions.stem: Probe placement on a dependent limb can affect SpO2 how?
questions.explanation: Dependent positioning can introduce venous pulsations into the optical signal and falsely lower SpO₂. The cited volunteer study reported decreases as large as 8 percentage points; this is a study observation rather than an expected change in every patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 260

questions.stem: On this curve, which numbered point is in the region where a large PaO2 drop barely changes SpO2?
questions.explanation: Point 3 lies on the flat upper portion of the dissociation curve. In this region, a substantial PaO₂ decrease may produce little change in saturation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 253, 266

questions.stem: At which numbered point does a small PaO2 change produce the largest SpO2 change?
questions.explanation: Point 1 lies on the steep portion of the curve. A small PaO₂ change there produces a larger saturation change than at the flatter upper points.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: A patient on 100% O2 sits at point 3. A circuit leak drops PaO2 by half. What will SpO2 show at first?
questions.explanation: On the upper plateau, falling PaO₂ may initially cause little SpO₂ change. The supplied curve has no numerical axes, so it cannot establish that halving PaO₂ at point 3 necessarily stays on that plateau.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 253, 266

questions.stem: Which development helped pulse oximetry become a routine operating-room standard of care by 1986?
options: Affordable, easy-to-use LED sensors and microprocessor improvements
A requirement for repeated manual calibration by technicians
A new billing code that mandated the device
Replacement of all arterial blood gas testing
questions.explanation: LED-based sensors and digital microprocessors made pulse oximeters easier to use and less expensive, supporting their rapid operating-room adoption. The textbook dates their acceptance as a standard of care to 1986; it does not attribute adoption primarily to proven mortality benefits.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 11, printed pp. 254–255 (complete revised question and answer set independently verified)

questions.stem: Which patient is at highest risk of PACU desaturation?
options: Thin adult after a superficial procedure
Obese elderly patient after extensive surgery
Healthy young patient after a short procedure
Child after myringotomy breathing room air comfortably
questions.explanation: Obesity, advanced age, and extensive surgery are associated with significant PACU desaturation in the cited study. Among the choices, the elderly obese patient after extensive surgery combines these risk factors.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 265

questions.stem: Why is pulse oximetry important during recovery in the postanesthesia care unit (PACU)?
options: Patients may develop hypoxemia during recovery
questions.explanation: Patients can develop hypoxemia during recovery as residual anesthetic effects and airway obstruction persist. Pulse oximetry supports continued assessment but does not replace direct observation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 265

questions.stem: Respiratory gas monitoring helps confirm which of the following?
options: Cardiac output and circulating blood volume
questions.explanation: Respiratory gas monitoring helps assess oxygen reaching the breathing system, ventilation, and anesthetic-agent concentrations. Together with pressure and volume alarms, it also helps detect equipment problems; it does not directly establish tissue oxygen delivery or cardiac output.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed pp. 211, 213; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Ventilator alarms indicating low pressure most likely point to:
questions.explanation: A substantial leak can prevent the circuit from reaching the expected airway pressure. Low-pressure alarms therefore prompt a check for leaks or disconnection and assessment of actual ventilation.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: High pressure alarms with normal volumes most likely point to:
questions.explanation: During volume control, increased airway resistance can raise pressure while tidal volume is maintained. A kink or other obstruction is therefore consistent with this alarm pattern.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166

questions.stem: On machine spirometry, which variables can appear on either axis?
questions.explanation: Flow, volume, and pressure can be plotted against one another on either axis of respiratory loops. Time is conventionally the horizontal axis when a time-based curve is displayed.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 230

questions.stem: With mechanical ventilation, flow-time curves often appear in which shapes?
questions.explanation: Volume control commonly uses a square inspiratory flow waveform, while pressure control and pressure support commonly show decelerating flow. Other patterns exist, so the expected tracing depends on the selected mode and settings.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed pp. 230–231

questions.stem: Which hemoglobin species are in the denominator of fractional saturation but not functional saturation?
questions.explanation: Fractional saturation includes COHb and MetHb in the total hemoglobin denominator. Functional saturation uses only oxyhemoglobin plus reduced hemoglobin, excluding those dyshemoglobins.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: A patient with significant methemoglobinemia has an SpO2 that won't rise with more O2. What explains this?
options: MetHb is invisible to the oximeter
MetHb can’t carry O2 but alters absorption
MetHb increases O2 binding to Hb
MetHb improves perfusion at the probe
questions.explanation: Methemoglobin’s ferric iron cannot bind oxygen normally, and its optical absorption distorts the two-wavelength SpO₂ estimate. With substantial MetHb, the reading tends toward about 85% and may not reflect improvements in arterial oxygen tension.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed pp. 257–258; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 629

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury is transported intubated. EtCO2 drifts from 35 to 50 mmHg. What is the concern?
options: No concern; this is permissive hypercapnia
questions.explanation: Rising arterial CO₂ dilates cerebral vessels and can increase cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure. A rising end-tidal trend during transport therefore warrants reassessment of ventilation, with arterial confirmation when needed because the gradient may change.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 247–248

questions.stem: Which three physiologic processes can influence the CO₂ concentration measured by capnography?
options: It reflects ventilation, perfusion, and metabolism
It measures arterial O2 tension directly
questions.explanation: Exhaled CO₂ reflects the interaction of alveolar ventilation, pulmonary perfusion, and metabolic CO₂ production. Capnography provides information about all three, but does not replace other monitors or directly measure arterial oxygen tension.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 10, printed pp 239, 249 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which two mechanisms account for most intraoperative heat loss? Select 2.
questions.explanation: Radiation is the largest route of heat loss to the environment, followed by convection. Redistribution can rapidly lower core temperature after induction, but it transfers heat within the body rather than itself removing body heat.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 290–291

questions.stem: Which are consequences of perioperative hypothermia? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Hypothermia impairs coagulation and immune defenses, increasing bleeding and wound-infection risk. It also slows drug handling and can prolong neuromuscular blockade.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which are intermediate temperature sites? Select 3.
questions.explanation: The cited classification places rectal, bladder, and oral measurements in the intermediate group. They may estimate core temperature but become less reliable during rapid thermal changes, and bladder accuracy depends strongly on urine flow.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: Which statements about neuraxial anesthesia and temperature are correct? Select 3.
options: Patients may not feel cold despite hypothermia
Threshold reduction scales with block height
It has less effect than GA
It spares vasoconstriction below the block
questions.explanation: Neuraxial anesthesia can reduce the sensation of cold and lower vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds in proportion to block height. Because peripheral vasoconstriction is impaired, core temperature may continue falling without the usual plateau.

questions.stem: Which features point to serotonin syndrome rather than NMS? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Clonus and hyperreflexia support serotonin toxicity, and symptoms can develop rapidly after a serotonergic drug exposure or change. The inspected text gives onset from minutes up to 24 hours, so it does not verify a strict six-hour distinction or the complete three-answer comparison with NMS.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 14, printed pp. 213–214

questions.stem: Which reduce cutaneous heat loss intraoperatively? Select 3.
options: Underbody warmer set high under the back
questions.explanation: Cotton blankets reduce heat loss, forced-air warming transfers heat to the patient, and a warmer room reduces the temperature gradient to the environment. Turning an underbody heater high is not a general solution: heat over poorly perfused pressure areas can cause injury.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 294–295
